newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Exchange trade in Russia shares to raise liquidity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Exchange trade in Russia shares to raise liquidity.

text.p: The Russian Trading System (RTS), a NASDAQ-like electronic equities market accounting for about half of total Russian share trading, faces a challenge from rival exchanges planning to trade stocks, but analysts say the outcome could be increased trading volumes generally.
The RTS is run by the national brokers' association NAUFOR, which won a battle in 1994 with the dozens of stock and commodity exchanges in Russia for the lion's share of equities trading.
Most of the stock and commodity exchanges were actually little more than glorified wholesale markets, trading anything from sacks of cement to crates of soft drinks.
But a few survived by moving into futures on currencies or more conventional commodities such as sugar and oil.
Three exchanges have now flung down a new challenge to the RTS and plan to start trading equities.
The officially backed Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) is looking for a new role as its share of the tightly regulated currency market is dwindling.
It is the official floor for the large and transparent government securities market, but wants to branch out into equities. MICEX plans to trade utility Mosenergo, Rostelekom and Norilsk Nickel.

The Russian Exchange, which was the main floor for trading privatisation vouchers in 1993 but now specialises in futures, has recently launched spot and futures trading in LUKoil, Mosenergo and Rostelekom, as well as a futures contract on the RTS index.
And Moscow's ambitious mayor Yuri Luzhkov intends to launch a Moscow Stock Exchange to trade shares.
RTS index futures are also traded at the St Petersburg Futures Exchange and the Siberian Stock Exchange in Novosibirsk.
RISE IN SHARE VOLUME EXPECTED
Traders and analysts said average daily turnover was now running at about $100 million, split between the RTS and over-the-counter trading.
This would increase when the exchanges start to operate as the shares they have chosen are the most liquid ones, they said.
NAUFOR listing committee director Alexander Kuzetenko told Reuters the rise in volume would be due to simpler technology.
"At some point securities with stable volumes will have to be traded at an exchange providing simpler technology," he said.
"Brokers will not need to be traders and analysts at the same time, as they have to in the RTS. They will just have to push buttons."
Alexei Telyatnikov, director of the PAUFOR technical centre, which operates RTS on behalf of the NAUFOR brokers' association, said he was not afraid of market fragmentation.
"Market volume is not growing in the blue chips, but in less liquid shares and growth is pretty stable," he said.
But he acknowledged that the RTS could initially see lower volumes in the shares traded on other exchanges.
"Maybe our turnover in these paper will become smaller, but they will never be completely gone," he said. "We shall always be dedicated to medium-liquidity paper."
Exchange trading will raise liquidity by speeding up registration, the key problem for the Russian market, he said.

"Liquidity here does not depend on the number of trading floors, but the speed of the clearing system," he said. "The market is coming to the point where an electronic clearing system will be necessary."

On MICEX, for instance, shares will be registered at the end of the trading day, but putting a new shareholder's name into a register will take several days, said Marina Medvedeva, MICEX stock department head.
On RTS it takes between three to 15 days to re-register shares, Telyatnikov said.

MICEX plans to introduce an order-driven system of trading in which similar bids and offers match automatically. The Russian Exchange is working on a double auction system, where bids find the best offers automatically.
SOME TRADERS SCEPTICAL ABOUT FUTURE OF EXCHANGES
Troika Dialog chief trader Alexei Dolgikh is sceptical about the future of equity trading at the exchanges.
"I cannot see which exchanges can deal in them seriously," he said. "They do not have a good clearing system, they do not have money. I am suspicious about the exchanges except MICEX."
Rinaco Plus vice-president Viktor Agroskin said the MICEX rule requiring a 100 percent deposit for money and paper before trading may restrict high trade volumes.
"The success of MICEX trading will depend on the willingness of market participants to leave funds there for a long time. And that will depend on how cheap money is for them," he said.

Under such a scheme Russian banks, which have cheaper funds than brokerages, have most advantages, Agroskin said. On the other hand, banks mostly manage their own funds, while brokerages have more foreign clients.
"The question is whether foreign clients would like to leave funds in roubles on MICEX for such a long time. Volumes will depend on that," he said.
